quotes.t: Leisure without books is death, and burial of a man alive.
Man, the living creature, the creating individual, is always more important than any established style or system.
The fish in the water is silent, the animal on the earth is noisy, the bird in the air is singing. But man has in him the silence of the sea, the noise of the earth and the music of the air.
Your idol is shattered in the dust to prove that God's dust is greater than your idol.
Man is a born child, his power is the power of growth.
He who has overcome his fears will truly be free.
The least initial deviation from the truth is multiplied later a thousandfold.
It is easy to perform a good action, but not easy to acquire a settled habit of performing such actions.
Never put off till tomorrow what may be done day after tomorrow just as well.
The difference between the almost right word and the right word is really a large matter - 'tis the difference between the lightning-bug and the lightning.
A classic is something that everybody wants to have read and nobody wants to read.
People who succeed have momentum. The more they succeed, the more they want to succeed, and the more they find a way to succeed.
You see, in life, lots of people know what to do, but few people actually do what they know.
The secret of success is learning how to use pain and pleasure instead of having pain and pleasure use you.
Your vision will become clear only when you can look into your own heart.
The creation of something new is not accomplished by the intellect but by the play instinct.
Loneliness does not come from having no people around you, but from being unable to communicate the things that seem important to you.
I have found that among its other benefits, giving liberates the soul of the giver.
When someone shows you who they are, believe them the first time.
The desire to reach for the stars is ambitious. The desire to reach hearts is wise.
It is absurd to divide people into good and bad. People are either charming or tedious.
I have the simplest tastes. I am always satisfied with the best.
A man who does not think for himself does not think at all.
Freedom is not worth having if it does not include the freedom to make mistakes.
It is unwise to be too sure of one's own wisdom. It is healthy to be reminded that the strongest might weaken and the wisest might err.
Action expresses priorities.
A pessimist sees the difficulty in every opportunity; an optimist sees the opportunity in every difficulty.
Attitude is a little thing that makes a big difference.
We shall defend our island, whatever the cost may be.
Do not fear death.
Never be jealous.
Do not let yourself be guided by the feeling of lust or love.
What we have once enjoyed deeply we can never lose. All that we love deeply becomes a part of us.
Character cannot be developed in ease and quiet. Only through experience of trial and suffering can the soul be strengthened.
Never bend your head. Always hold it high. Look the world straight in the eye.
The art of war teaches us to rely not on the likelihood of the enemy's not coming, but on our own readiness to receive him.
He will win who, prepared himself, waits to take the enemy unprepared.
There is no instance of a nation benefitting from prolonged warfare.
We are what our thoughts have made us; so take care about what you think.
All differences in this world are of degree, and not of kind, because oneness is the secret of everything.
The fire that warms us can also consume us; it is not the fault of the fire.
Just as a well-filled day brings blessed sleep, so a well-employed life brings a blessed death.
He who loves practice without theory is like the sailor who boards ship without a rudder and compass and never knows where he may cast.
The greatest deception men suffer is from their own opinions.
We are all born with a divine fire in us. Our efforts should be to give wings to this fire and fill the world with the glow of its goodness.
Climbing to the top demands strength, whether it is to the top of Mount Everest or to the top of your career.
One best book is equal to a hundred good friends, but one good friend is equal to a library.
Cheers to a new year and another chance for us to get it right.
I believe that every single event in life happens in an opportunity to choose love over fear.
Breathe. Let go. And remind yourself that this very moment is the only one you know you have for sure.
The purpose of life is to live it, to taste experience to the utmost, to reach out eagerly and without fear for newer and richer experience.
It isn't enough to talk about peace. One must believe in it. And it isn't enough to believe in it. One must work at it.
One thing life has taught me: if you are interested, you never have to look for new interests. They come to you.
Talk to a man about himself and he will listen for hours.
What we anticipate seldom occurs; what we least expect generally happens.
Seeing much, suffering much, and studying much, are the three pillars of learning.
It takes a long time to become young.
I am fundamentally an optimist. Whether that comes from nature or nurture, I cannot say. Part of being optimistic is keeping one's head pointed toward the sun, one's feet moving forward.
A casual stroll through the lunatic asylum shows that faith does not prove anything.
Kind words do not cost much. They never blister the tongue or lips.
The future has several names. For the weak, it is impossible; for the fainthearted, it is unknown; but for the valiant, it is ideal.
The hunger for love is much more difficult to remove than the hunger for bread.
There is but one truly serious philosophical problem and that is suicide.
Time you enjoy wasting is not wasted time.
The greatest griefs are those we cause ourselves.
You see things; you say, 'Why?' But I dream things that never were; and I say, 'Why not?'
The best way to keep one's word is not to give it.
I don't know what your destiny will be, but one thing I know: the only ones among you who will be really happy are those who have sought and found how to serve.
To know the road ahead, ask those coming back.
Fear is a natural reaction to moving closer to the truth.
Beware the barrenness of a busy life.
If a man does not keep pace with his companions, perhaps it is because he hears a different drummer.
To carry yourself forward and experience myriad things is delusion. That myriad things come forth and experience themselves is awakening.
Common sense is not so common.
We can easily forgive a child who is afraid of the dark; the real tragedy of life is when men are afraid of the light.
Culture is the widening of the mind and of the spirit.
The ultimate measure of a man is not where he stands in moments of comfort and convenience, but where he stands at times of challenge and controversy.
Dwell in possibility.
The pain of parting is nothing to the joy of meeting again.
By failing to prepare, you are preparing to fail.
Boredom: the desire for desires.
Hatred does not cease by hatred, but only by love; this is the eternal rule.
Don't let the noise of others' opinions drown out your own inner voice.
Henceforth I ask not good-fortune, I myself am good-fortune.
If you do not tell the truth about yourself you cannot tell it about other people.
Vanity and pride are different things, though the words are often used synonymously.
I am not an angel, and I will not be one till I die: I will be myself.
Medicine is my lawful wife and literature my mistress.
Man is fond of counting his troubles, but he does not count his joys.
If you hate a person, you hate something in him that is part of yourself.
Live the questions now. Perhaps you will then gradually, without noticing it, live along some distant day into the answer.
Give me books, French wine, fruit, fine weather and a little music out of doors, played by somebody I do not know.
Happiness makes up in height for what it lacks in length.
Love takes off the masks that we fear we cannot live without and know we cannot live within.
Those who have a 'why' to live, can bear with almost any 'how'.
The cosmos is within us. We are made of star-stuff. We are a way for the universe to know itself.
Life is not easy for any of us. But what of that? We must have perseverance and above all confidence in ourselves.
Power concedes nothing without a demand. It never did and it never will.
I can shake off everything as I write; my sorrows disappear, my courage is reborn.
Life, although it may only be an accumulation of anguish, is dear to me, and I will defend it.

A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.bio: Indian aerospace scientist and the 11th President of India (2002-2007), known as the 'Missile Man of India'.

Albert Camus.bio: French-Algerian writer and philosopher, author of The Stranger; Nobel Prize in Literature 1957.

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

Anton Chekhov.bio: Anton Chekhov was a Russian playwright and master of the short story, a practising doctor who wrote The Cherry Orchard, Uncle Vanya and hundreds of stories. His restrained, humane art reshaped both the theatre and short fiction of the 20th century.

Aristotle.bio: Greek philosopher and student of Plato; founder of logic and many scientific fields.

Benjamin Disraeli.bio: British statesman who served twice as Prime Minister and led the Conservative Party. He was also a successful novelist, writing books such as Coningsby and Sybil.
Benjamin Disraeli.credit: Cornelius Jabez Hughes, Public domain (File: File:Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield.jpg)

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Blaise Pascal.bio: French mathematician, physicist and philosopher, author of the Pensées.
Blaise Pascal.credit: unknown; a copy of the painting of François II Quesnel, which was made for Gérard Edelinck en 1691, Public domain

Bruce Lee.bio: Bruce Lee was a Hong Kong-American martial artist and actor who transformed martial-arts cinema with films such as Enter the Dragon. His philosophy of adaptability — 'be water' — blended Taoist ideas with his own Jeet Kune Do.
Bruce Lee.credit: National General Pictures, Public domain (File: File:Bruce Lee 1971 National General Pictures publicity photo.jpg)

Buddha.bio: The Buddha was an Indian teacher whose teachings on suffering, mindfulness, and compassion became Buddhism, followed by hundreds of millions.

Carl Jung.bio: Swiss psychiatrist who founded analytical psychology. His concepts of the collective unconscious, archetypes and introversion and extraversion remain influential in psychology and culture.
Carl Jung.credit: AnonymousUnknown author, Public domain (File: File:CARL JUNG (1875 - 1961).jpg)

Carl Sagan.bio: American astronomer and beloved science communicator. His television series Cosmos (1980) and books such as Pale Blue Dot brought astronomy to a worldwide audience.

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Charlotte Bronte.bio: Charlotte Brontë was an English novelist and poet, the eldest of the Brontë sisters. She is best known for Jane Eyre (1847), published under the pen name Currer Bell, a landmark of English literature.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Eleanor Roosevelt.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt was the longest-serving First Lady of the United States, from 1933 to 1945, and reinvented the role as a platform for civil rights and social reform. Afterward she became a US delegate to the United Nations and chaired the commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
Eleanor Roosevelt.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain (File: Eleanor Roosevelt portrait 1933.jpg)

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Frederick Douglass.bio: American abolitionist and writer who escaped slavery and became a leading voice against it.

Friedrich Nietzsche.bio: German philosopher known for Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the concept of the will to power.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

George Bernard Shaw.bio: Irish playwright and critic; author of Pygmalion; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925.
George Bernard Shaw.credit: Sussman, Public domain (File: George Bernard Shaw, playwright (SAYRE 9001).jpg)

Helen Keller.bio: American author and activist who, deaf and blind from childhood, became a renowned advocate for disability rights.
Helen Keller.credit: Los Angeles Times; restored by User:Rhododendrites, Public domain

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Hermann Hesse.bio: Hermann Hesse was a German-Swiss novelist and poet whose works explore self-discovery and spirituality, including Siddhartha, Steppenwolf and The Glass Bead Game. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1946.

James Baldwin.bio: American writer known for Go Tell It on the Mountain and the essay collection Notes of a Native Son.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

John Lennon.bio: English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles and solo artist known for Imagine.

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Leonardo da Vinci.bio: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance painter, engineer and anatomist whose notebooks reveal an insatiable curiosity about nature and art. He painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and filled thousands of pages with studies, inventions and observations.
Leonardo da Vinci.credit: Leonardo da Vinci, Public domain (File: Leonardo self.jpg)

Mahatma Gandhi.bio: Leader of India's nonviolent independence movement; pioneered satyagraha and became the father of the Indian nation.

Marie Curie.bio: Marie Curie was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who pioneered the study of radioactivity, a term she coined. She remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911 — and died of illness caused by her long exposure to radiation.

Mark Twain.bio: American writer (Samuel Clemens) known for Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and The Adventures of Tom Sawyer.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Maya Angelou.bio: American poet and memoirist best known for I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969).
Maya Angelou.credit: Bee Photos by Ryan Marty, Public domain

Miyamoto Musashi.bio: Legendary Japanese swordsman, undefeated in over sixty duels, author of The Book of Five Rings and the Dokkodo.

Mother Teresa.bio: Albanian-Indian Catholic nun who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata; Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1979).
Mother Teresa.credit: John Mathew Smith & www.celebrity-photos.com from Laurel  Maryland, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Nelson Mandela.role: Anti-apartheid leader, President of South Africa
Nelson Mandela.bio: South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison and became the country's first Black president in 1994.

Oprah Winfrey.bio: American talk-show host and media executive whose long-running show made her one of the most influential broadcasters in history.
Oprah Winfrey.credit: US Embassy South Africa, Public domain

Oscar Wilde.bio: Irish playwright, poet and author of The Picture of Dorian Gray, famed for his wit and epigrams.
Oscar Wilde.credit: Napoleon Sarony (restoration by Adam Cuerden), Public domain

Pablo Picasso.bio: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who co-founded Cubism and reinvented his style across a career of nearly eighty years. Works such as Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and Guernica made him the most famous and influential artist of the 20th century.
Pablo Picasso.credit: Didier Descouens, Public domain (File: File:(Barcelona) Retrat de Picasso - Pablo Gargallo - Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya.jpg)

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Rabindranath Tagore.bio: Bengali poet and polymath from India; the first non-European Nobel laureate in Literature (1913), known for Gitanjali.

Rainer Maria Rilke.bio: Rainer Maria Rilke was an Austrian poet born in Prague, author of the Duino Elegies and the Sonnets to Orpheus. His Letters to a Young Poet, advising patience and solitude, have guided generations of artists; he wrote in German and later in French.

Robert Frost.bio: American poet known for depictions of New England rural life; four-time Pulitzer Prize winner.
Robert Frost.credit: Unknown author at the source., Public domain

Seneca.bio: Roman Stoic philosopher and statesman, author of Letters to Lucilius.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Sun Tzu.bio: Ancient Chinese general traditionally credited with The Art of War, a treatise on strategy studied worldwide for over two thousand years.
Sun Tzu.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: 吴司马孙武.jpg)

Swami Vivekananda.bio: Indian Hindu monk who introduced Vedanta and Yoga to the West; famous for his 1893 Chicago Parliament of Religions address.
Swami Vivekananda.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: Swami Vivekananda at Parliament of Religions.jpg)

Tony Robbins.bio: Tony Robbins is an American author, coach and motivational speaker known for bestselling books such as Unlimited Power and Awaken the Giant Within. His seminars and self-help programmes have made him one of the most prominent figures in the personal development industry.

Victor Hugo.bio: French poet and novelist, author of Les Misérables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.
Victor Hugo.credit: Étienne Carjat, Public domain (File: Victor Hugo by Étienne Carjat 1876 - full.jpg)

Viktor Frankl.bio: Viktor Frankl was an Austrian psychiatrist and Holocaust survivor who founded logotherapy, a form of psychotherapy centred on the search for meaning. His book Man's Search for Meaning (1946), drawn from his experiences in Nazi concentration camps, has sold millions of copies worldwide.

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

Walt Whitman.bio: American poet best known for the collection Leaves of Grass (1855).

Winston Churchill.bio: British prime minister during the Second World War and Nobel laureate in Literature.
